Thebes. The major city of Boeotia in central Greece rose from cultural obscurity to become a military superpower under Epaminondas in the fourth century BCE. Famous in mythology as the cursed city of Oedipus and the site of tragic cycles, Thebes challenged Athens and Sparta for hegemony through innovative tactics and became the first city to defeat Sparta in open battle.

Thebes was the legendary home of Oedipus, the tragic king who unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy by killing his father and marrying his mother. According to myth, the city itself was founded by Cadmus, a Phoenician hero, who sowed dragon's teeth from which armed warriors sprang from the earth. The city housed the Sacred Band of Thebes, an elite regiment of three hundred hoplites paired as lovers. Their bond was thought to strengthen their fighting power and make them invincible on the battlefield.

Epaminondas was a brilliant military commander who developed the oblique phalanx tactic and defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE, shattering the myth of Spartan invincibility. This victory elevated Thebes to supreme power in Greece. The city served as a center of Boeotian power and culture, situated between Athens and Sparta, often caught in their regional rivalry.

Thebes hosted the Mysteries of Cabiri, secret religious rites, and was an intellectual center in its own right. The city was destroyed and its people enslaved by Alexander the Great in 335 BCE for resisting Macedonian rule, becoming a cautionary example of resistance to conquering powers.

Epaminondas was the military genius who elevated Thebes to supreme power. Oedipus was the mythological hero and king associated with the city's curse. Athens was the northern neighbor and frequent rival in regional politics. Sparta was defeated by Thebes at Leuctra under Epaminondas. Alexander the Great, the conqueror, destroyed the city as punishment for its defiance.
